summary: Defines the use of IRIs and URIs to identify or interact with entities that communicate via XMPP. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 5122.

eli5.summary: Web links like xmpp:name@place let you point to a chat user or room. This defines how those links are written.

questions: how do i link to an xmpp user
subtitle: URLs and internationalized links for instant messaging and presence systems

tldr.problem: XMPP applications need a standard way to identify entities and trigger actions using web-style URLs, supporting international characters and various interaction modes.
tldr.mechanism: The xmpp: URI scheme wraps XMPP addresses (like user@server) into URLs that can be clicked in web browsers and other non-native applications, with support for queries, authentication, and internationalized characters.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now link to XMPP entities reliably, though the scheme was superseded by RFC 5122 which improved the specification.

today: RFC 4622 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 5122, which improved the specification based on experience and deployment feedback.

sections.title: What XMPP IRIs and URIs Do
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is a protocol for real-time messaging. Inside an XMPP network, addresses look like email addresses: user@example.com or user@example.com/resource. However, these addresses cannot be used directly in web browsers, calendars, or other non-XMPP applications.

This RFC defines how to turn XMPP addresses into Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs) and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) that web browsers and other programs understand. An XMPP URI looks like xmpp:user@example.com and can be embedded in web pages, emails, or used by applications to trigger XMPP actions.

The RFC serves two purposes: identifying XMPP entities ("here is an XMPP user") and interacting with them ("open a chat window to this user").
sections.eli5: XMPP addresses are like phone numbers inside a messaging system. This RFC turns them into web links that anyone can click, even if they do not use XMPP directly.

sections.title: Syntax and Components
sections.content:
An XMPP IRI or URI has the basic form xmpp:address, where the address is a standard XMPP address. The address may include a node (user name), domain (server), and optional resource (the specific connection or device). Examples include xmpp:user@example.com to identify a user on a server, xmpp:user@example.com/laptop to identify a specific device or session, and xmpp:example.com to identify just the server.

More advanced forms support an authority component (with //) to specify credentials: xmpp://user@example.com/contact@example.com signals the application to authenticate as user before sending to contact.

Query components use the ? character for actions. For example, xmpp:user@example.com?message tells the application to open a message compose window. Key-value pairs follow, separated by semicolons: xmpp:user@example.com?message;subject=Hello. Fragment identifiers (using the number sign character) are allowed but their meaning is application-specific.
sections.eli5: An XMPP link starts with xmpp: and then the address. You can add extra info with ? to say send a message or // to say log in as someone first.

sections.title: Supporting World Languages
sections.content:
XMPP addresses can contain nearly any Unicode character, including accents, Chinese characters, and other scripts. Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs) let you write these directly, while URIs must encode non-ASCII bytes as percent-encoded sequences like %C5%99.

For example, a Czech address like jiří@český.example/v Praze becomes the IRI xmpp:jiří@český.example/v%20Praze (with the space percent-encoded) and the URI xmpp:ji%C5%99i@%C4%8Dechy.example/v%20Praze. Applications must handle conversion between IRIs and URIs using the rules from RFC 3987. Special characters that have meaning in URLs (such as the fragment identifier marker, question mark, slash, and at-sign) must be percent-encoded when they appear in the node or resource parts.
sections.eli5: If your name has special letters, the link spells them out carefully so programs everywhere can understand it.

sections.title: How Applications Use These Links
sections.content:
When a web browser or application encounters an xmpp: URI, it must extract the XMPP address, determine whether to authenticate differently (from the authority component), decode any percent-encoded characters, and then typically connect to an XMPP server.

The process is similar to how mailto: URLs work: click the link, and the application opens a compose window. With XMPP URIs, clicking a link may open a chat window, join a chat room, subscribe to presence information, or trigger other XMPP-specific operations defined in the query component. The RFC notes that if an application does not recognize a query type or key, it must ignore it gracefully.

For reliability, resources like user@example.com/iphone are temporary (they represent a specific login session) while addresses like user@example.com and servers like example.com are more permanent. This affects how long an XMPP URI can reliably point to the same entity.
sections.eli5: When you click an XMPP link, the app reads it, connects to the messaging system, and does what the link asked (like opening a chat with that person).

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
XMPP URIs expose addressing information: putting xmpp:user@example.com on a public website makes it easy for spam robots to harvest addresses. Due care should be taken when publishing XMPP links on public sites.

The RFC prohibits passwords in the authority component, since XMPP uses the SASL protocol for authentication and can support anonymous login if needed. However, the authority component itself reveals which user the application will authenticate as, which may or may not be safe to expose.

A semantic attack is possible because users familiar with web URLs expect // after the scheme, but in XMPP URIs the // introduces the authority component (for authentication), not the path. So xmpp://user@example.com (with //) means "authenticate as user", while xmpp:user@example.com (without //) just identifies the user. Applications should clearly show users which form they are using.

IRIs support the full Unicode range, which could enable address spoofing if a domain example.cοm (with a Cyrillic 'o') looks identical to example.com (with a Latin 'o'). Applications must follow best practices to prevent such "phishing" attacks.
sections.eli5: Be careful: posting chat links on websites lets robots spam those users. Also, // in a link has special meaning, and similar-looking letters can trick people.
